keyVerseText: Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house, and delivered them into the hand of his servants: and king Asa sent them to Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus, saying,
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun חֶזְיוֹן (Chezyôwn) derives from the root חָזָה (châzâh), which means to see, behold, or prophesy. This root conveys not merely physical sight but also the mental and spiritual act of perceiving or receiving a vision, often in a prophetic or revelatory context. Thus, the literal sense of חֶזְיוֹן encompasses the idea of an inspired or divine vision, adding depth beyond the simple English term "vision" by implying a supernatural or revelatory insight.
usageInScripture: The word חֶזְיוֹן appears only once in Scripture, specifically in 1 Kings 15:18, where it functions as a proper name, identifying the grandfather of Ben-hadad, king of Syria. In this context, the translation "of Hezion" reflects a genealogical marker rather than a direct reference to a vision or prophetic experience. This usage demonstrates the word's flexibility, serving both as a common noun meaning "vision" and as a personal name, likely rooted in the concept of seeing or revelation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חֶזְיוֹן as rooted in the concept of divine vision enriches our grasp of biblical revelation and prophecy, emphasizing that God's truth is often communicated through supernatural sight or insight. Even when used as a proper name, the connection to seeing or vision reminds believers that God's sovereign plans unfold through His revealed will. This underscores the importance of spiritual perception in the life of faith, encouraging Christians to seek God's guidance and revelation. Moreover, the fact that this term names a king's ancestor highlights how God's sovereign purposes extend through history and human lineage, ultimately fulfilled in Christ as the ultimate revelation of God.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 15:18, the phrase "Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria" uses חֶזְיוֹן to anchor Benhadad's lineage and royal legitimacy. This genealogical detail, "of Hezion," situates the narrative within historical and political realities, reminding readers that God's unfolding plan interacts with real human families and rulers. The name's root meaning of "vision" subtly points to God's providential oversight even in the affairs of foreign kings, underscoring that God's sovereign vision governs all history.
